study.title: Exodus 9 The plagues, the hardness of the heart, and the sovereignty of the LORD
study.overview: Exodus 9 describes three successive plagues in Egypt: the death of the cattle of the field, the ulcers on men and animals, and the hail with thunder and fire. At each stage, the text emphasizes that the Lord distinguishes Israel from Egypt, protects its people in Goshen and makes it clear that Pharaoh is dealing not only with natural phenomena, but with the living God who judges, preserves and rules the whole earth. The chapter also shows Pharaoh's oscillation: for a moment he acknowledges guilt, asks for prayer and promises deliverance, but then returns to obstinacy.

outline.title: The fifth plague: the death of Egyptian cattle
outline.explanation: The LORD proclaims a plague against the flocks in the field, preserves the beasts of Israel, and fulfills his word the next day. Even before the verification that the cattle of the Hebrews were not attained, Pharaoh remains hardened.

outline.title: The sixth plague: ulcers on men and animals
outline.explanation: Moses casts as a grey into the air as a sign of the new plague. The wounds hit Egyptians and even the Magi, who can no longer stand before Moses. The chapter records that the LORD confirms Pharaoh's hardening.

outline.title: New warning and the chance to fear the word of the Lord
outline.explanation: The LORD announces a series of more severe judgments, that Pharaoh may know that there is none other like Him, and that his name be known in all the earth. Some of the king's officers fear the divine word and collect the cattle, while others despise the warning.

outline.title: The seventh pest: hail, momentary confession and final indentation
outline.explanation: Hail falls with thunders and fire, destroying men, animals, plantations and trees, except in Goshen. Pharaoh confesses sin, asks for prayer and promises to deliver the people, but after the thunder ceases to sin and reaffirm their hardness.

study.context: The chapter is set in the context of the confrontation between the God of Israel and Pharaoh in Egypt. The text presupposes the presence of the Hebrews in the Egyptian territory and mentions Goshen as the region where they lived. The activity of the Egyptian magicians also appears, now powerless in the face of the plague of ulcers. The notes provided highlight the distinction between Israel and Egypt and suggest that the Egyptian gods linked to power and fertility are shown to be incapable before the LORD.
study.theology: Exodus 9 teaches that the Lord is sovereign over the life, health, climate and fertility of the earth. The plagues are not only punishments, but also revelations: they show that there is no other like the LORD in all the earth, and that his name must be known among the nations. The chapter also highlights human responsibility before the word of God. Some officers of Pharaoh fear and act; Pharaoh sees, confesses momentarily and goes back. Thus, the narrative unites judgment and mercy, warning and opportunity, making it clear that repeatedly resisting the word of God hardens the heart even further.

scholarViews.insight: The distinction between the cattle of Israel and that of Egypt shows that a natural explanation is only insufficient; the plague points to the direct action of the LORD on the flocks.
The plague of ulcers reaches the bodies of the Egyptians themselves when smaller judgments have not produced effect, showing that God can intensify discipline when there is persistent resistance.
The magicians cannot stand before Moses because of the wounds, which shows the complete defeat of human and spiritual opposition before the power of God.

questions: What aspects of Pharaoh's heart appear when he recognizes guilt, but does not remain in repentance?
How does the separation between Goshen and the rest of Egypt help to understand the righteousness and protection of God?
How does the reaction of Pharaoh's servants contrast with the king's stubbornness, and what does this teach about hearing the word of the LORD?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to take the word of God seriously before resistance becomes a habit. The concrete application is to examine areas in which obedience is postponed, confesses only under pressure or reacts only after suffering consequences. It also calls us to trust that God distinguishes his people, preserves those who belong to him and governs even what seems out of control. A practical answer is to obey promptly what has already been revealed in the Scriptures, rather than expecting harsh circumstances to force us to do so.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not explain all the details of the pests or authorize conclusions about natural causes, dates or geography beyond what the text mentions. There is also a limitation in Matthew Henry's notes in 9:13, which appear truncated; therefore, the synthesis of this point was made only with the excerpt available. Where commentators offer theological readings, they were presented as interpretations, not as indisputable conclusions of the text.
